name: Mercury skin creams

card.summary: Inorganic-mercury creams used to lighten skin tone and fade dark patches by suppressing pigment, a practice with documented toxicity and widespread bans.
card.aka: mercuric chloride creams, mercury skin lightening
card.note: Banned in many countries; mercury compounds are linked to kidney and neurological harm.

quick.overview:
Mercury skin creams contain inorganic mercury salts, such as mercuric chloride, used to lighten skin tone and fade blemishes. People who use skin lighteners seek a paler or more even complexion, and mercury has been used for this purpose since at least antiquity.

Today mercury in cosmetics is illegal in many countries, but products containing it are still reported on the market, sometimes without it being listed on the label. Interest in skin whitening, including searches for mercury creams, has grown worldwide over the past decade.
quick.how: The creams are applied to the face or body as a topical lightener, typically over weeks or months. Mercury accumulates in the skin's deeper layers and interferes with pigment production, which is how it lightens tone.
quick.risks: Health authorities and reviews associate mercury lighteners with kidney damage and neurological effects, and prolonged use can discolour the skin. Mercury exposure also reaches household members and, during pregnancy, the fetus. Many countries prohibit it in cosmetics.

lead: Mercury skin creams are topical products with inorganic mercury compounds as the active ingredient, used to lighten complexion and reduce dark spots [1]. Mercury-containing cosmetics date back to ancient Greece and Rome, where bleaching preparations often included mercury and white lead [1].

The goal is a lighter or more even skin tone. Skin whitening is most prevalent in Africa and Asia, and a Google Trends analysis covering 2013 to 2023 found global interest in skin whitening and in hydroquinone and mercury creams rising [2]. Reports say some lighteners still contain concealed mercury, and surveys in 2013 found that 77 percent of Nigerian women reported using lightening products [1].

Documented health effects include kidney damage and neurological problems; mercury accumulating in the dermis can itself discolour skin [1]. Mercury in these products is illegal in multiple countries, yet studies continue to find it in products sold [1].

angle.text: People use these creams to lighten overall skin tone or fade patches of hyperpigmentation. The lightening is documented, as are the toxic effects that have led many regulators to ban the compound in cosmetics.

paras: Ancient Greek and Roman cosmetics for whitening often contained mercury, and in the 1800s American women used products with toxic levels of lead and mercury [1]. Mercury ointments were also used in dermatology until recently [3].

South Africa began banning mercury and high-hydroquinone products in the 1970s [1]. In the UK many skin whiteners are illegal but still sold, and trading standards bodies lack resources to address this [1].

The Google Trends study found searches for skin whitening most popular in Sudan, Vietnam and Sri Lanka, and searches for hydroquinone cream exceeded those for mercury cream in nearly all countries except the Philippines and Indonesia [2].

No studies found of mercury creams as an effective treatment. Related published work is epidemiological and toxicological: a historical paper examined mercury ointments as a possible cause of the composer Bedrich Smetana's hearing loss, citing mercury ototoxicity [3].

Acute mercury toxicity can cause pneumonitis and gastric irritation; long-term exposure may cause kidney damage, insomnia, memory loss and irritability [1]. The WHO has noted inorganic mercury in skin products is associated with skin cancer [1].
